---
title: "Events: the page talks back"
---

In the previous chapter your button counted clicks through an `onclick` attribute
glued into the HTML. It worked, and it was a stopgap. Real pages hand the job
to TypeScript, and by the end of this chapter yours does too.

## Click and watch the console {#sec-events-experiment}

Create a new app from our template and open it in
VS Code. In `index.html`, add one button below the heading:

```html
<button id="helloButton" type="button">Say hello</button>
```

The `type="button"` says that this button submits nothing. Leave it out and
`npm run check` complains, so make it a habit.

Now delete everything in `src/index.ts` and type these four lines:

```ts
const helloButton = document.getElementById('helloButton') as HTMLButtonElement;

helloButton.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  console.log(event);
});
```

The first line is the starter's own pattern: `as HTMLButtonElement` tells
TypeScript which kind of element the id stands for. Every kind has such a
name, `HTMLDivElement` for a `div`, `HTMLParagraphElement` for a `p`, and VS
Code offers them as you type. The chapter on types for elements replaces this
line with something better; copy it as it is until then.

Start the app with `npm start`, open the page, and open the developer tools
with `F12`. Switch to the Console tab and click the button a few times.

Every click prints one line. Chrome writes `PointerEvent {isTrusted: true, ...}`,
Firefox writes `click { target: button#helloButton, ... }`. Different browsers,
same idea. Click the small triangle in front of the line and the object folds
open into a long list of properties.

## The browser calls your function {#sec-events-callback}

Read your four lines again. Nowhere do you call the arrow function. You hand it
over to `addEventListener`, your program ends, and the browser calls the
function later, once for every click.

Last year p5.js did the same thing, and in the starter project you even saw
the handover. The frame at the top of `src/index.ts` connected your functions
to the sketch, one per line:

```ts
const p = new p5((sketch: p5): void => {
  sketch.setup = setup;
  sketch.draw = draw;
  sketch.mouseClicked = mouseClicked;
});
```

You wrote `mouseClicked`, you never called it, and p5.js called it on every
click. All the p5.js names lived on one object, which is why every command got
`p.` in front of it.

The browser works the same way, with one object called `document` in place of
`p`, and the page's elements hanging below it. Two things differ. p5.js had
one fixed slot per event, `sketch.mouseClicked`, and the whole canvas was one
surface. The browser has no fixed slots: you name the element, the event, and
the function yourself in one `addEventListener` call, and you can attach as
many functions to as many elements as you like.

So a function can travel as a value. Until now you passed numbers, strings, and
arrays into functions; here the argument *is* a function. Writing
`(event) => { ... }` right inside the call is the short way, and it is not the
only way. A function you declared somewhere in the file works just as well, as
long as you pass its name:

```ts
function onHelloClick(event: MouseEvent): void {
  console.log(event.clientX, event.clientY);
}

helloButton.addEventListener('click', onHelloClick);
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The parentheses that break everything

`addEventListener('click', onHelloClick())` runs your function immediately,
once, and hands the browser whatever came back. TypeScript catches that one and
reports that a value of type `void` is not a listener. Drop the parentheses,
pass the plain name, and the error goes away.
:::

## What is inside the event {#sec-events-object}

The object the browser passes in describes one thing that happened. Open the
logged event in the console and look for `type`, which holds the string
`'click'`, and for `target`, which is the element the event started on. That
target is the very same object `helloButton` points at, one element with two
names.

Two more properties are worth knowing by heart. `event.clientX` and
`event.clientY` hold the position of the mouse pointer in pixels, counted from
the top left corner of the browser window. Log them, click in different corners
of the button, and watch the numbers move.

A mouse event carries a couple of dozen more properties, and the book will not
list them. MDN does that better, on its pages about
[the Event interface](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Event)
and [the MouseEvent interface](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MouseEvent).

Buttons are not the only things that fire events. The whole document does. When
the user presses a key anywhere on the page, `document` gets an event, and that
event object has a `key` property holding what was pressed.

## Colors straight from TypeScript {#sec-events-style}

HTML says what is on the page. How it looks, its colors, sizes, and fonts, is
the job of a second language called **CSS**, short for Cascading Style Sheets.
CSS gets its own chapters later in this part; for now you only need to know
that every element object has a `style` property, and through it you set CSS
from your code:

```ts
helloButton.style.backgroundColor = 'tomato';
```

CSS writes that property as `background-color`, with a hyphen in the middle.
Hyphens are not allowed in TypeScript names, so the DOM spells the same
property `backgroundColor`. The pattern holds for the rest of CSS too, with
`fontSize` for `font-size` and `borderRadius` for `border-radius`.

Setting properties one by one from code is the quickest way to see a change,
and it is not how a real page is styled. A later chapter in this part moves the
look into a stylesheet and leaves only the changing parts in TypeScript. For
now, `tomato` on a button is enough of a reward.

## A number that survives the click {#sec-events-counter}

A counter has to remember something between two clicks, so the variable belongs
outside the listener:

```ts
let clickCount = 0;

helloButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
  clickCount += 1;
  helloButton.textContent = `Clicks: ${clickCount}`;
});
```

`src/index.ts` runs once, when the page loads. It creates `clickCount`,
registers the listener, and finishes. The arrow function stays behind and can
still see `clickCount`, because it was written next to it, and every call adds
one to that same variable.

Move `let clickCount = 0;` inside the listener and the counter is built fresh on
every click, so the button shows `Clicks: 1` forever.

This listener declares no parameter at all, because nothing inside it needs the
event. Leave out what you do not use. The compiler reports parameters you
declare and never touch.

::: {.research title="Which event do you need?"}
The exercise below needs a box that notices the mouse pointer arriving and
leaving, and a paragraph that shows the key the user just pressed. Picking the
right event name is the everyday work here, and the book stops explaining at
this line.

1. Name the two mouse events that fire when the pointer moves onto an element
   and when it moves off it again.
2. A key goes down and comes back up. Name the two keyboard events for those
   two moments, and say which of them fires first.
3. The user presses the Enter key. What exactly does `event.key` hold then?

Exams run without internet and without an AI, so the names of the events you
use every week belong in your head.
:::

## Exercise: a page that reacts {#sec-events-exercise}

::: {.callout-note}
## When a step does not make sense

The exercises grow with every chapter, and sooner or later a step description
will not make sense to you. Get as far as you can on your own first. In
school, ask your teacher. At home, ask an AI: paste your code and the step
you do not understand, and say what you tried. You can also ask the coding
buddy you set up in Part 1, which knows this course. Asking well is not
cheating. Describing a problem so precisely that
an AI can help is a skill every developer needs today, and every stuck step
is a chance to practice it.
:::

Build a page with a button that counts clicks, a box that reacts to the
mouse, and a line that shows the last key you pressed. Work through the 
steps in order and check the result of each one in the browser before you 
go on.

1. Create a new app from our template and open the
   folder in VS Code.

2. In `index.html`, replace the `<h1>` line with this markup. Leave the
   `<script>` tag underneath exactly as it is.

   ```html
   <h1>A page that reacts</h1>
   <button id="counterButton" type="button">Clicks: 0</button>
   <div id="colorBox">Hover me, click me</div>
   <p id="keyEcho">Press any key</p>
   ```

   Run `npm start`. The page shows a button, a line of text, and a second line
   of text.

3. Delete the contents of `src/index.ts` and get the three elements:

   ```ts
   const counterButton = document.getElementById('counterButton') as HTMLButtonElement;
   const colorBox = document.getElementById('colorBox') as HTMLDivElement;
   const keyEcho = document.getElementById('keyEcho') as HTMLParagraphElement;
   ```

   VS Code marks all three as unused. That warning disappears in the next
   steps.

4. Give `counterButton` a click listener that counts up and writes the count
   into the button's own text, in the form `Clicks: 3`. Keep the counter
   variable outside the listener. This is the counting button from the previous
   chapter again, this time without the `onclick` attribute in the HTML.
   Clicking now raises the number in the button by one.

5. Under the three `const` lines, declare an array named `colors` with at
   least four CSS color names, and a `let` variable named `colorIndex` that
   starts at `0`. Then add a click listener to `colorBox` that paints the box
   with the color at `colorIndex` and adds one to `colorIndex`. Write the
   painting as two lines, because TypeScript cannot prove that `colorIndex`
   stays inside the array and refuses the direct assignment:

   ```ts
   const nextColor = colors[colorIndex];
   if (nextColor) {
     colorBox.style.backgroundColor = nextColor;
   }
   ```

   The first click paints the whole stripe across the page, since a `div`
   without a stylesheet takes the full width of the window. The fourth click
   is the last one that changes anything: after that, `colorIndex` points past
   the end of the array, `nextColor` is `undefined`, and the `if` skips the
   assignment. The chapter on types for elements comes back to values that
   might be missing.

6. Make the colors wrap around. When `colorIndex` reaches the length of the
   array, set it back to `0`. An `if` does it, and so does the `%` operator
   from last year. Clicking now walks through your colors and starts over
   after the last one.

7. Give `colorBox` two more listeners, so that its text reads `Ready` while the
   pointer is on the box and `Hover me, click me` again once the pointer has
   left. Your research task has the two event names. Moving the mouse across
   the box now swaps the text back and forth, and the background color stays
   whatever your clicks made it.

8. Add a listener to `document` that writes the key the user just pressed into
   `keyEcho`, in the form `You pressed: a`. The paragraph must update while the
   key is still down, not when it comes back up, and your research task says
   which of the two events that is. Press `a` and the paragraph reads
   `You pressed: a`. Every key fires the event, the modifier keys included, so
   try a few and watch what comes out.

9. Add one `if` to that listener: when the user presses the Enter key, write
   `Press any key` into the paragraph instead. Your research task says what
   `event.key` holds for that key. After Enter, the paragraph looks like it did
   when the page loaded.

10. Run `npm run check` and fix what Biome reports.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Stuck on an event name?

Type the event as a string into `addEventListener` and let VS Code help. The
editor knows the list and offers it while you type, which is faster than a
search and works in the exam too.
:::

Six short questions: the three from the research task, and three about
listeners. One or two sentences are enough for each.
